description:
S.O.M.A (Selenographic Observation & Mission Atlas) 

We are building a Tradespace analysis tool for Luna in a way that helps mission engineers plan and choose landing sites on the southern pole of Earth's moon. The trade space analysis tool sits as a Python library and a demo web application, which computes and fetches information about communication relays, sunlight illumination, orbital advantages, terrain data and much more. This is a research-focused project.
summary: S.O.M.A. (Selenographic Observation & Mission Atlas) is a research-grounded Python library and web planning tool for evaluating lunar landing scenarios and data-delivery options near the Moon’s south pole. Given a candidate landing location, operating date, dataset size, deadline, terrain, communication, and power assumptions, SOMA models local horizons and visibility, sunlight and solar generation, lander battery and storage limits, direct-to-Earth and relay contacts, and finite-capacity store-and-forward schedules. It then produces an auditable, explainable plan showing when data is transmitted, where it waits, which relay path is used, and whether delivery is feasible under the declared assumptions. The project addresses the challenge by connecting landing-site and date selection to the operational realities that determine whether a mission can communicate and preserve energy. Its Python library, reproducible exports, independent replay checks, and visual lunar interface make trade studies easier to compare, explain, and verify before mission design decisions are made.
details:
S.O.M.A. (Selenographic Observation & Mission Atlas)

What the project does

S.O.M.A. is a terrain-aware lunar communications and power planner. It takes a proposed landing location, operating date, dataset size, delivery deadline, lander configuration, and network assumptions, then produces an explainable plan for moving that data from the Moon to Earth. The result shows when transmission can occur, which direct or relay contact is used, where data waits between contacts, when the final data arrives, and whether the modeled energy reserve remains within its limit.

How it works

  1. Scenario definition: The Python engine validates JSON inputs, coordinate and frame metadata, units, UTC timestamps, finite storage, radio limits, battery settings, and declared resource profiles.
  2. Lunar geometry: The physical model uses matched DE421 lunar reference frames, ephemeris and leap-second data, Moon-fixed surface coordinates, numerical LOLA terrain, local horizons, and finite-range visibility checks.
  3. Illumination and power: Terrain and solar geometry determine sunlight at the lander. A fixed-panel model estimates generation, while battery replay accounts for base load, transmission, storage, and waiting.
  4. Communications and scheduling: Geometric opportunities become usable contacts with finite capacity, endpoint service time, storage limits, and causal forwarding. The scheduler compares direct-to-Earth and store-and-forward relay paths against the dataset volume and deadline.
  5. Verification and presentation: The engine exports the scenario, inputs, schedule, energy history, provenance, and checksums. Independent replay checks whether the reported allocation satisfies the same constraints. The browser interface presents lunar geometry, contacts, timelines, and captured results through a Cesium-based view.

Benefits and intended impact

S.O.M.A. connects a landing site and date to an operational question that engineers can inspect: can this lander deliver this dataset by this deadline without exhausting its modeled energy reserve? It lets a team compare candidate sites, dates, relay choices, terrain assumptions, and power configurations using the same declared inputs. The output is meant to support early mission trade studies, communication planning, education, and review. A result means feasible under the stated inputs and model. It is not a flight certification or a claim that a real network reservation exists.

Tools, data, and resources used

Software and implementation: Python 3.12+, the SOMA Python package and CLI, JSON schemas, a local HTTP service, GitHub for source control, a Cesium Moon client for visualization, and Mintlify for the public library documentation. No physical hardware was required. Hardware behavior is represented through declared lander battery, solar-panel, radio, storage, base-load, and relay profiles.

NASA data and resources: the NASA Space Apps Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge brief; NASA SPICE lunar frame and kernel documentation; NASA Goddard’s South Pole LOLA DEM Mosaic; the NASA Planetary Data System LOLA south-polar elevation product; NASA NTRS material on improved LOLA landing-site elevation maps, contact multigraph routing, LunaNet, and Moon Trek. These sources support the challenge alignment, lunar geometry, terrain, illumination, communication, and visualization methods.

Other sources and tools: the Tradespace Analysis Toolkit for Constellations (TAT-C) and its model-centric engineering paper; the LuSEE-Night power-generation study; distributed space-ground resource coordination research; the CCSDS Schedule-Aware Bundle Routing specification; the Queqiao-2 lunar relay study; and Cesium Moon. The project records whether an input is measured, published, synthetic, or assumed so that a captured demonstration is not mistaken for complete physical validation.

What is creative about it

S.O.M.A. combines terrain visibility, sunlight, battery state, contact capacity, storage, relay forwarding, and deadline scheduling in one inspectable delivery plan. Its distinctive output is not only a map or a visibility window. It explains the complete path of a finite dataset, including the periods when the data must wait and the energy cost of waiting. The same calculation can run from Python or through the browser workflow, and the exported record can be replayed independently.

Attached resources

The project package includes the Vercel demo website, research paper, Mintlify Python library documentation, GitHub repository, and YouTube demonstration linked below.

Research paper: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1utqXAAPHZXsVH62VVNJ9ALWGAbCJk-eG/view?usp=drive_link

GitHub repository: https://github.com/darthvader58/soma

Mintlify Python library documentation: https://soma-ce3178ca.mintlify.site/

Vercel demonstration: https://soma-atlas-two.vercel.app

YouTube demonstration: https://youtu.be/ZSkentUd6DU
